noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand that the central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord and is linked to sense organs by nerves
understand that stimulation of receptors in the sense organs sends electrical impulses along nerves into and out of the central nervous system, resulting in rapid responses

primer.text: You already know that sense organs detect changes around you. This note maps the wiring that turns detection into action: the brain and spinal cord at the centre, nerves radiating outward, and electrical impulses sprinting along neurones. Learn the pathway vocabulary here — it repeats in every reflex and sense-organ question later in the course.

lessons.title: Structure of the nervous system
lessons.opening: The nervous system splits into a central part — the brain and spinal cord — and a peripheral part of nerves reaching every corner of the body. Information travels as fast electrical impulses along cells called neurones, and a nerve is simply a bundle of those neurones. The central section processes incoming signals and coordinates the reply.
keyPoints: The central nervous system is the brain plus the spinal cord.
The peripheral nervous system is every nerve branching from the centre to the rest of the body.
Neurones carry electrical impulses; a nerve is a bundle of neurones.
Nerves reach the sense organs, letting the brain communicate with all body regions.

low.restatement: Two divisions: the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) does the processing, and peripheral nerves carry messages to and from it.
low.analogy: Think of a headquarters with roads leading to every town — the headquarters decides, the roads deliver.
low.examPointer: Spell out the CNS abbreviation on first use: examiners want 'central nervous system — brain and spinal cord' as the full phrase.

medium.restatement: Electrical impulses along neurones give the system its speed; bundled neurones form nerves that link the central coordinating centre to sense organs and effectors.
medium.analogy: Nerves are broadband cables made of many wires (neurones), so losing one wire rarely cuts the whole connection.
medium.examPointer: Questions award the mark for 'bundle of neurones' — do not call a nerve a single cell.

check.stem: Which structures make up the central nervous system?

options.text: The brain and the spinal cord
options.explanation: Those two structures form the CNS.

options.text: All the nerves of the body
options.explanation: That describes the peripheral nervous system.
Sense organs feed the CNS; they are not it.

options.text: The heart and major blood vessels
options.explanation: That is the circulatory system, a different topic.

options.text: A single neurone stretching the body's length
options.explanation: One neurone is one cell; nerves contain many.
A nerve is defined as a bundle of neurones.

options.text: A muscle that moves the spine
options.explanation: Nerves carry signals, they are not contractile tissue.
Neurotransmitters are the chemicals; nerves are structures.

check.stem: How does information travel through the nervous system?

options.explanation: Fast-moving electrical signals pass along neurones.

options.text: As hormones diffusing through the blood
options.explanation: That is hormonal communication, the slower parallel system.

options.text: As food molecules absorbed by cells
options.explanation: Nutrition has no signalling role here.

options.text: As sound waves through the bones
options.explanation: Sound only matters inside the ear as a stimulus.

check.stem: Which role does the central nervous system play in a response?

options.text: It detects the stimulus at the body surface
options.explanation: Receptors in sense organs do the detecting.

options.text: It contracts to move the limbs
options.explanation: Muscles move limbs; the CNS instructs them.

options.text: It processes incoming information and coordinates the body's response
options.explanation: The CNS is the central coordinating centre.

options.text: It stores energy for the response
options.explanation: Energy storage belongs to liver and adipose tissue.

check.stem: Why do nerves reach the sense organs?

options.text: So receptors there can send impulses into the CNS and receive instructions back
options.explanation: The link carries impulses both into and out of the centre.

options.text: To supply the eyes with oxygen
options.explanation: Blood vessels, not nerves, supply oxygen.
Glands lubricate; nerves signal.

options.text: To anchor the organs in place
options.explanation: Connective tissue anchors; nerves connect.

check.stem: State the two components of the central nervous system.
check.modelAnswer: The brain and the spinal cord.

check.stem: Name the cells that carry electrical impulses, and the bundles they form.
check.modelAnswer: Neurones carry the impulses, and bundled together they form nerves.

check.stem: Explain why electrical signalling suits the rapid responses the specification describes.
check.modelAnswer: Electrical impulses travel along neurones at high speed, so a stimulated receptor can alert the CNS and trigger an effector within a fraction of a second — far faster than chemical transport through blood, which is why nervous responses are described as rapid.

check.stem: A student's fingertip touches something sharp. List, in order, the structures the signal passes through between the skin and the muscle that pulls away.
check.modelAnswer: Receptors in the skin fire sensory impulses along sensory neurones into the CNS, which processes them and sends motor impulses along motor neurones to the effector muscles that withdraw the finger.

lessons.title: Function: receptors, impulses and rapid responses
lessons.opening: Detection starts when receptors in a sense organ are stimulated — by light, sound, touch, temperature or chemicals. The receptors fire electrical impulses that race along sensory neurones into the central nervous system, which replies through motor neurones to effectors. Because the signal is electrical, the whole loop runs in a fraction of a second.
keyPoints: Receptors in sense organs detect stimuli such as light, sound, touch, temperature and chemicals.
Sensory neurones carry those impulses into the central nervous system.
Motor neurones carry instructions out to effectors — muscles that contract or glands that secrete.
The relay from receptor through sensory neurone and CNS, then motor neurone to effector, produces a rapid response.

low.restatement: A stimulus fires receptors; impulses flow in along sensory neurones, the CNS decides, and motor neurones instruct effectors to respond.
low.analogy: It is a call centre: the hotline (sensory) brings the complaint in, the operator decides, the dispatch line (motor) sends the fix.
low.examPointer: Practise writing the full pathway in order — sequence marks are lost when a step is skipped.

medium.restatement: The pathway runs in one direction per arc: input neurones enter the centre, output neurones leave it, and the electrical medium makes the round trip nearly instantaneous.
medium.analogy: Like a roundabout with one-way lanes — inbound traffic never mixes with outbound, so nothing slows the loop.
medium.examPointer: Do not write 'nerves think' — award language is 'CNS processes the information and coordinates the response'.

check.stem: What do receptors produce when a sense organ is stimulated?

options.explanation: Stimulation makes receptors generate electrical impulses.
Glands release hormones; receptors fire impulses.
No cells are created during detection.
Receptors consume, not produce, oxygen.

check.stem: Which neurones carry impulses into the CNS?

options.explanation: Sensory neurones are the inbound line to the CNS.
Motor neurones carry instructions outward.
Relay neurones work inside the CNS, not from the sense organs.
Effectors are muscles and glands, not neurones.

check.stem: Which list of stimulus types matches the sense organs named in this note?

options.explanation: These are the detected stimulus classes.
Not part of the IGCSE sense-organ list.
The list is wider than the two obvious senses.
Taste and smell are chemicals, but the other stimuli count too.

check.stem: What do effectors do once instructed by motor neurones?

options.explanation: Those are the two effector actions named.
The actions are matched to the wrong tissue types.
Effectors act; they do not build detector cells.

options.text: They send impulses back to the sense organ
options.explanation: Effectors are the endpoint, not another relay.

check.stem: Why is the receptor-to-effector loop described as automatic and rapid?

options.text: Because the impulses travel electrically along neurones without conscious routing
options.explanation: Electrical speed plus fixed pathways gives rapid automatic responses.

options.text: Because each step waits for a hormone to arrive
options.explanation: Hormonal transport is the slower system.

options.text: Because the CNS asks the brain to decide consciously each time
options.explanation: Conscious decision would make it slow and voluntary.
Impulses originate at receptors, not effectors.

check.stem: State the direction sensory neurones and motor neurones each carry impulses.
check.modelAnswer: Sensory neurones carry impulses into the CNS; motor neurones carry them out to effectors.

check.stem: Name the two effector actions produced at the end of the pathway.
Explain why impulses travel in both directions — inward and outward — during a nervous response.
check.modelAnswer: The CNS cannot act on a stimulus it has not received, so sensory neurones bring impulses in from the receptors; once it has processed that information it must instruct effectors, so motor neurones carry impulses back out — the two directions are the input and output halves of one loop.

check.stem: A bright torch flashes into someone's eyes and their pupils narrow. Identify the receptor, the processing centre and the effector in this response.
check.modelAnswer: Light receptors in the retina are stimulated, the CNS processes the incoming impulses, and circular muscles in the iris are the effectors whose contraction narrows the pupils.

glossary.definition: The brain and spinal cord together — the coordinating centre of the nervous system.
A specialised cell that carries electrical impulses; bundled neurones form nerves.
A neurone carrying impulses from receptors in the sense organs into the central nervous system.
A neurone carrying impulses from the central nervous system out to effectors.

figures.alt: Diagram of the nervous system showing the CNS with brain and spinal cord, nerves, a nerve cross-section, and a neuron with labelled parts.
figures.caption: The central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord and is linked to sense organs by nerves which are bundles of neurones
